[RECORD] Plaintiff is a 67-year-old Black man.
[RECORD] Plaintiff checked into a motel in Atlanta.
[RECORD] Motel manager called police and reported plaintiff as a 'suspicious person' after seeing him in the lobby.
[RECORD] Police officers arrived, asked plaintiff to leave, and when he refused, arrested him for trespass.
[RECORD] Plaintiff was held for 9 hours and released without charges.
[LAW] Under 42 U.S.C. § 1983, a person may be held liable for deprivations of constitutional rights caused by a government official acting under the color of state law.
[LAW] A false arrest claim requires a showing that the arresting officers lacked probable cause for the arrest.
[LAW] The legality of the arrest depends on whether the police had probable cause to believe the plaintiff had committed a crime.
[INFERRED] If the motel manager's report was the sole basis for the arrest, and there was no other evidence of criminal activity, the arrest may have been without probable cause, potentially violating the plaintiff's Fourth Amendment rights.
[INFERRED] Whether the motel manager's report of the plaintiff as a 'suspicious person' and the subsequent arrest by police officers for trespassing violated the plaintiff's constitutional rights under 42 U.S.C. § 1983.

A false arrest claim requires a showing that the arresting officers lacked probable cause for the arrest (Groman v. Township Of Manalapan, 51 F.3d 140, 145 (1st Cir. 1995)).
[INFERRED] The plaintiff was arrested for trespassing after the motel manager reported him as a 'suspicious person.' The legality of the arrest depends on whether the police had probable cause to believe the plaintiff had committed a crime. If the motel manager's report was the sole basis for the arrest, and there was no other evidence of criminal activity, the arrest may have been without probable cause, potentially violating the plaintiff's Fourth Amendment rights (John Betts v. Martha Anne Shearman, 752 F.3d 136, 141 (2d Cir. 2014)).
[INFERRED] Based on the available information, it is unclear whether the arrest was supported by probable cause. Further evidence is needed to determine whether the plaintiff's constitutional rights were violated under 42 U.S.C. § 1983.

[INFERRED] The opposing party would argue that the arrest was justified by probable cause, as the motel manager's report of the plaintiff as a 'suspicious person' could reasonably support the officers' belief that the plaintiff had committed trespass. Under [LAW] federal law, probable cause is a complete defense to a claim of false arrest under 42 U.S.C. § 1983 (John Betts v. Martha Anne Shearman, 752 F.3d 136, 141 (2d Cir. 2014)). Furthermore, even if the arrest was based on insufficient evidence, the officers may be shielded by qualified immunity if they had arguable probable cause (Jones v. [LAW] Probable cause is an absolute bar to a claim of false arrest asserted under the Fourth Amendment and section 1983 (946 F.3d 342, 353).
[INFERRED] The plaintiff must establish that the private motel manager's actions were sufficiently connected to the police response to constitute state action under § 1983.

[INFERRED] Whether a private motel and its manager can be held liable under 42 U.S.C. § 1983 for a guest's arrest, and whether the officers' subsequent arrest constitutes false arrest when the guest refused to leave.
[INFERRED] To state a claim under 42 U.S.C. § 1983, a plaintiff must show that the conduct causing the deprivation of a federal right was fairly attributable to the State (457 U.S. 922, 937). Furthermore, the existence of probable cause or the lawful request to leave a premises can serve as a defense or bar to false arrest claims under § 1983 (946 F.3d 342, 353).
[INFERRED] Here, the plaintiff is a 67-year-old Black man who checked into a motel in Atlanta and was reported as a 'suspicious person' by the manager, leading police to ask him to leave and subsequently arresting him for trespass when he refused. While the plaintiff suffered a deprivation of liberty by being held for 9 hours and released without charges, establishing liability against the private motel under § 1983 requires satisfying the state action requirement, such as joint action or state compulsion. Additionally, because the officers asked him to leave and he refused, the resulting trespass arrest implicates potential probable cause defenses that bar false arrest claims under § 1983.
[INFERRED] The § 1983 claim against the motel faces significant hurdles regarding the state action requirement and potential probable cause defenses for the arrest, requiring further factual development regarding police involvement and the manager's instigation.
[INFERRED] The opposing party would argue that the § 1983 claim fails as a matter of law because a private motel and its manager are not state actors, and merely summoning police or reporting a suspected trespass does not convert private conduct into state action under the Fourteenth Amendment.
[LAW] Conspiracy or joint action in § 1983 actions is required to draw in private parties who would otherwise not be susceptible to a § 1983 action because of the state action doctrine (398 U.S. 144, 152).
[INFERRED] Furthermore, even if state action could be established, the officers' independent decision to arrest the plaintiff after he refused a lawful request to leave the premises establishes probable cause, which serves as an absolute bar to any false arrest or wrongful detention claim under § 1983.
